title: Solid hexagon motif
subtitle: A six-sided motif worked in two rounds from the centre
excerpt: A small solid hexagon worked in rounds of treble, with a single chain at each of the six corners. Two rounds make a coaster-sized motif in DK cotton. Hexagons tile together with no gaps, which makes them a favourite for blankets and bags.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the crochet hexagon worked in rounds (Fig. 442). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The magic-ring start and the DK-cotton gauge are modernised; the six-corner round structure is Victorian.

chartDefinition.caption: Read each round outward from the magic-ring centre. A single chain sits at each of the six corners; the sides fill solid with treble.

glossaryTerms.definition: An adjustable starting loop for working in the round. The first round is worked into the ring, then the tail is pulled to close the centre tight with no hole.
The gap left under one or more chains. Here a single chain sits at each of the six corners; the next round works into that space.
Wetting or steaming the finished motif and pinning it to shape while it dries, so the six sides sit even and the same size as the others.

content.text: The hexagon is the six-sided cousin of the square, and it tiles together with no gaps, which makes it a favourite for blankets and bags. This one is worked solid, with treble filling each side and a single chain at each corner to turn it. Two rounds make a coaster-sized motif in DK cotton, starting from a
magic ring
. The pattern is written in UK terms, where treble is the tall everyday stitch (double crochet in the United States).
What you need
DK cotton, one colour.
About 14 m makes one hexagon. A mercerised DK cotton such as Drops Paris or Scheepjes Cahlista shows the stitches cleanly. Any DK yarn works, though cotton holds the shape best.
A 4 mm hook.
The standard DK pairing. Adjust by half a millimetre either way to hit the size if your tension runs loose or tight.
Tapestry needle, scissors, and a blocking surface.
For weaving in the tails and setting the hexagon even.
Gauge

Rounds 1 and 2 make a hexagon about 9 cm point to point in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook, blocked. The first round should measure about 4 cm across. Match the size on a single motif before making a set, so the pieces join cleanly.
Abbreviations
ch = chain
tr = treble (UK), called double crochet in the US
sl st = slip stitch
sp = space; st, sts = stitch, stitches
Pattern
Read the chart from the centre outward, alongside the written rounds. The chart shows the six corners; the written rounds give the counts.
Round 1.

Form a magic ring. Ch 3 (counts as the first treble), 2 tr into the ring, ch 1, [3 tr into the ring, ch 1] 5 times. Sl st to the top of the ch 3 to join, then pull the tail to close the ring. This makes six groups of 3 tr with a
chain space
at each corner. (18 sts)
Round 2.

Sl st into the next ch-1 corner space. Ch 3 (counts as the first treble), then 2 tr, ch 1, 3 tr all into the same corner space. [1 tr in each of the next 3 tr, then work 3 tr, ch 1, 3 tr all into the next ch-1 corner space] 5 times. 1 tr in each of the next 3 tr. Sl st to the top of the ch 3 to join. (54 sts)
Fasten off, leaving a 10 cm tail. The hexagon is complete.
Finishing
Weave the start and end tails into the back with the tapestry needle, doubling back once to lock each, then trim. Pin the hexagon out to even sides and
block
it, then leave to dry. Even blocking is what lets a set of hexagons sit flat together.
What to try next

Add a third round, working 9 tr along each side between the corners, for a 13 cm hexagon. A set of hexagons joins into a honeycomb blanket or a soft project bag. Worked in two colours, one for the centre round and one for the outer, the corners read as a clear six-pointed star.
